overview: The Hittite kingdom ruled from central Anatolia and became a major power in Syria during roughly 1650 to 1200 BCE. Hattusha was its capital. The map starts before this kingdom and repeats a large outline long after its collapse: its 2000 to 500 BCE span must not be read as one continuously surviving empire.

periods.title: Before the kingdom
periods.summary: Earlier Anatolian communities preceded the Hittite kingdom.

periods.title: Anatolian kingdom
periods.summary: Hattushili I established his capital at Hattusha; campaigns reached Syria and Babylon.

periods.title: Imperial expansion
periods.summary: Suppiluliuma I strengthened Hittite power and established a royal center at Carchemish.

periods.title: After the empire
periods.summary: Central rule ended around 1200 BCE. Smaller successor states continued parts of its political and cultural traditions.

sections.title: A capital and an international power

items.text: Hittite armies reached far beyond the Anatolian plateau. Murshili I raided Aleppo and Babylon, but was assassinated after returning home. Later kings rebuilt imperial strength. Control depended on changing campaigns, royal centers and agreements with neighboring rulers; the repeated map outline cannot show those shifting relationships.

At Hattusha, the defensive circuit stretched for more than eight kilometers. The Upper City had a double wall with over a hundred towers. Carved lions guarded one entrance, while a stone tunnel passed beneath the great artificial bastion at the Sphinx Gate. Arriving at the capital involved some impressive architecture.

The archive preserves a peace agreement between the Hittites and Egypt, usually called the Qadesh treaty. Alongside diplomacy, its clay tablets recorded laws, commerce, religion and stories. A government could need both an agreement with a rival king and instructions for a festival, and both could end up on clay.

Royal women also participated in diplomacy. Queen Puduhepa had an official seal, and a surviving Akkadian letter was sent to her by the Egyptian queen Naptera. Their correspondence gives us named women communicating across the same international world as their royal husbands.

Keeping a capital supplied required storage as well as walls. Excavation has revealed buried granaries and artificial ponds. In the densely occupied Lower City, people lived close to the Great Temple; religious buildings, homes and practical installations all belonged to the same working city.

A low depression behind broad earth banks in Hattusha was once even proposed as a royal burial place. Coring in 2002 instead supported its interpretation as a water reservoir. Archaeologists still have to work out how separate installations supplied the city; this evidence does not establish running taps in every house.

Hittite law clause 10 required someone who injured another person to arrange care and supply a replacement worker during recovery. The offender also owed six shekels of silver and the doctor's fee. An injury could disrupt a household's livelihood, so the rule addressed both healing and unfinished work.

Marriage involved families and transfers of wealth. Clause 28 discusses a promised marriage, a competing match and who should repay the earlier bride payment. Both father and mother appear in the rule. Such texts reveal parental authority and economic obligations, while telling us much less about the daughter's own wishes.

Farm animals could produce very ordinary disputes. Clause 66 allowed owners to reclaim livestock that had wandered into somebody else's enclosure without treating the neighbor as a thief. The law even considered a pig getting into a field or grain heap. Keeping dinner away from somebody else's dinner was evidently a practical problem.

Children could learn a craft within their family, while outside training could cost money. A legal rule listed six shekels of silver for teaching trades such as carpentry, weaving or metalworking. Midwifery also belonged among skills passed through practical instruction. Education often meant learning how to do a job.

Scribal training demanded a different toolkit: hundreds of signs and the ability to compose official documents. One scribal family can be followed through four generations in the thirteenth century BCE. Learning began with simpler signs and small tablets before longer compositions. A family business might involve clay paperwork rather than a shop.

Chariot horses had carefully planned care. The Kikkuli training text describes exercise, feeding, watering, rest and treatments such as blankets or massages. Its surviving thirteenth-century BCE copy preserves an older training tradition associated with a specialist from Mitanni. These animals had a timetable, and someone had to follow it from early morning until late at night.

sections.title: Belief, writing and the empire's end

items.text: A silver drinking vessel from the fourteenth or thirteenth century BCE ends in the head and forelegs of a stag. Its maker attached the antlers and handle separately. Around the rim, people approach deities with offerings. The imagery suggests ceremonial use, making the cup both skilled metalwork and a miniature religious scene.

Hittite scribes adapted cuneiform from the Akkadian tradition. They combined syllable signs with signs representing whole words, and used the script for several languages, including Hittite, Luwian, Hurrian and Akkadian. A single archive therefore preserves several linguistic worlds. The language of a tablet cannot be identified merely by its wedge-shaped marks.

During an epidemic, King Mursili II appealed to the gods and said that people had been dying for twenty years. His prayers considered broken oaths and divine anger, while seeking relief for the country. The testimony preserves fear and a religious explanation; it does not identify the infection in modern medical terms.

A short Hittite writing sample from that prayer is “ki-i-ma ku-it i-ya-at-ten”, translated “What is this that you have done?” This is a scholarly transcription of cuneiform from KUB XIV 10 with KUB XXVI 86, not the original wedge shapes. The question addresses the gods: even a powerful king could sound bewildered.

Tree rings from central Anatolia indicate an unusually severe run of dry years around 1198 to 1196 BCE. Repeated crop failures could overwhelm stored supplies. Researchers connect this climatic stress with the era of imperial collapse, while emphasizing political pressures and uneven local outcomes. Drought is a possible contributor, not a complete explanation.

ending.text: The central Hittite state disintegrated around 1200 BCE. Evidence suggests Hattusha was emptied by its administration before later fires, rather than simply destroyed in one known invasion. Smaller successor kingdoms, especially toward northern Syria, preserved parts of Hittite political and cultural traditions. The map's 500 BCE endpoint is not the date this empire fell.
